correctness.rationale: The all-size reduction is a direct four-round classwise matching strategy; four total selections cannot exhaust a corresponding part of size at least four. Every case therefore reduces to one of the twenty sorted positive part-size triples bounded by four. The exact Hintikka recursion compares complete atomic diagrams and all possible next vertex choices; the proof reconstructs its equivalence to four-round EF play by induction. Independent full-vertex and orbit-compressed implementations agree on the complete twenty-input partition and produce nine distinct classes, including the anomalous merger. The maximal minimum vertex count is nine and the (3,3,3) class requires each part size at least three. Finite checks alone are not the infinite step: that comes from the four-round truncation proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The strongest plausible coverage comes from binary-graph/equivalence-relation results. The hyperedge relation is a quantifier-free reduct of complete multipartite graph adjacency, so graph equivalence implies hypergraph equivalence, not conversely. In particular the binary signature distinguishes the (2,2,3) and (2,3,3) profiles at rank four, whereas the ternary signature equates them. Hence binary graph classifications cannot directly supply the nine ternary-only theories. General k-hypergraph EF bounds do not entail the exact table.

value.rationale: This is a complete classification of a natural infinite family of 3-uniform hypergraphs in the weak, unlabeled hyperedge signature. It determines precisely which part-size information four nested quantifiers retain, exhibits the nonobvious merger of capped types (2,2,3) and (2,3,3), and proves a sharp nine-vertex family-internal representative bound. The distinction from richer binary multipartite graphs is structurally motivated by the need to reconstruct part membership through ternary incidence. The precise nine-type count and merger are not supplied by generic EF theory or edge-ideal formulas, and may guide logical reductions on higher-uniformity blow-ups.
